      <title>Japan FA’s Kozo Tashima to stand against Infantino for Fifa presidency</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/nov/05/japan-fa-head-kozo-tashima-stand-against-gianni-infantino-for-fifa-president</link>
      <description><ul><li><p>Tashima says he brings ‘honest, sound, upright attitude’</p></li><li><p>He is understood to have acted with the blessing of Uefa</p></li></ul><p>The Japan Football Association’s honorary president, Kozo Tashima, ⁠has announced his intention to stand against Gianni Infantino in March’s Fifa presidential election.</p><p>Tashima is the second challenger to declare in advance of the 18 November deadline after the former Tottenham defender Ramon Vega, although it remains unclear whether Vega has the backing of five of Fifa’s 211 member associations, which is required to take a place on the ballot in Rabat.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/nov/05/japan-fa-head-kozo-tashima-stand-against-gianni-infantino-for-fifa-president">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/nov/05/fifa-wants-womens-olympic-football-under-23s</link>
      <description><ul><li><p>IOC open to dialogue and Fifa wants input from others</p></li><li><p>Fifa concerned about fixture congestion and workload </p></li></ul><p>Fifa wants the International Olympic Committee to restrict the women’s Olympic football tournament to under-23s owing to concerns over fixture congestion and the workload of senior players.</p><p>The eligibility criteria for the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles has been set, with qualification tournaments having begun in some regions, so no change can be made until Brisbane 2032 at the earliest, but sources at both organisations have told the Guardian that they are open to dialogue.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/nov/05/fifa-wants-womens-olympic-football-under-23s">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Uefa faces political flashpoint over Sevastopol’s ascent in Russian football</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/nov/05/uefa-fifa-ukraine-crimea-sevastopol-promotion-russia-war</link>
      <description><p>Promotion to third tier for Crimean club would be clear violation of governing body’s rules amid conflict in Ukraine</p><p>Uefa and Fifa face a decisive test of their appetite to punish Russia’s integration of teams from illegally occupied Ukrainian territory after FC Sevastopol, from Crimea, won promotion to the country’s professional third tier.</p><p>Sevastopol were declared champions of group one in Football National League (FNL) 2B, in effect Russia’s fourth division, last month and are believed to have applied for a licence to compete at the level above. Should it be granted and they proceed to FNL 2A, it would appear a violation of Uefa rules that prohibit Crimean clubs from playing in competitions organised by the Russian Football Union (RFU). The governing body would come under severe pressure to extend sanctions on European football’s pariah state, whose club and national teams are banned from competing in international tournaments.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/nov/05/uefa-fifa-ukraine-crimea-sevastopol-promotion-russia-war">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Is there anything you would like to ask the former Ipswich, Rangers and England defender?</p><p>Terry Butcher has lived a full life in football.       <description><p>There were protests at Old Trafford and even though two academy products stood out, Michael Carrick’s future is far from safe</p><p>Green and yellow balloons bobbed around the Stretford End. Tennis balls rained down on the pitch in protest at the chronic, enduringly cinematic decline presided over by Manchester United’s ownership. Then came a reminder of the humble football’s extraordinary power to bend history, minds and wills. United’s <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/nov/03/manchester-united-roma-champions-league-match-report">players departed victorious</a> having somehow won the game within the game, separating themselves from the fog of unhappy context swirling on all sides and turning the second half into its own soaring, ripping story for the ages.</p><p>Will it be enough to save Michael Carrick, who was once again serenaded when minds wandered from the joint scourges of the Glazer family and Jim Ratcliffe?       <title>Unai Simón caps myth-making week with another extraordinary night | Sid Lowe</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/nov/02/unai-simon-athletic-club-la-liga-myth-making-week-la-liga</link>
      <description><p>Athletic’s win over Real Sociedad was culmination of six unique days for the Spain keeper after night at the Palladium</p><p>For the third time in six days everyone got to their feet to hand a standing ovation to Unai Simón, dressed in all black, before the world. Named the best men’s goalkeeper on the planet, holding the Lev Yashin trophy, they had applauded him at the London Palladium on Monday night and before the game began at San Mamés, Bilbao, on Sunday. Now somewhere in the middle of it all, the ferocity of the 197th Basque derby, there was another moment, even more meaningful and more lasting, a cheer again giving way to something deeper: an appreciation for a man as well as his work closing a week that will be forever his. Which means it will be forever theirs too.</p><p>Real Sociedad and Athletic Club had been doing battle for 72 minutes and it was 2-1 when Simon took off to make a save that denied Carlos Soler an equaliser <a href="https://x.com/LaLiga/status/2117010126544781601?a=D2pBmWmVdGI0IyB4-ec&amp;s=20">and defied belief</a>. As the ball flew off his palm, San Mamés exploded. And then it happened: never mind that Athletic still had a derby to win and a corner to defend, forget the fact that the lead was a single goal, the visitors relentless now and 25 minutes still to resist; at <a href="https://%20www.theguardian.com/football/blog/2013/sep/17/athletic-bilbao-sid-lowe">the stadium everyone calls the Cathedral</a>, a place of ritual and liturgy like no other, the entire congregation, 50,092 people, started clapping. Started and did not stop. For a minute, maybe more, it was like the match that matters most didn’t matter at all, momentarily fading until it was just him and them together.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/nov/02/unai-simon-athletic-club-la-liga-myth-making-week-la-liga">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Our NextGen picks from five years ago show that breaking through early does not guarantee longevity or future success</p><ul><li><p>Read the full updates on our class of 2021 <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/ng-interactive/2021/oct/07/next-generation-2021-60-of-the-best-young-talents-in-world-football">here</a> and <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/ng-interactive/2021/oct/06/next-generation-2021-20-of-the-best-talents-at-premier-league-clubs">here</a></p></li></ul><p>In 2021, as every year, we picked 80 players from around the world who had a chance of making it in world football – <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/ng-interactive/2021/oct/06/next-generation-2021-20-of-the-best-talents-at-premier-league-clubs">20 from the Premier League</a> and <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/ng-interactive/2021/oct/07/next-generation-2021-60-of-the-best-young-talents-in-world-football">60 from the rest of the world</a> – as part of our <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/series/next-generation">Next Generation series</a>.</p><p>We then follow these talented boys on their journeys for five years.       <link>https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/oct/26/mourinhos-plan-comes-together-as-real-madrid-relaunch-with-clasico-statement</link>
      <description><p>It was just like old times as José Mourinho ended a night at Camp Nou with a knee slide and three points</p><p>José Mourinho had already done the <em>por qu</em><em>é?</em>, <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/sep/21/real-madrid-atletico-madrid-jose-mourinho-diego-simeone-madrid-derby-la-liga">the printout</a> and the press conference no-show in under 100 days. Now he’s done a knee slide too, and in the perfect place: back where it all began and where it can all begin again. When Kylian Mbappé scored the first in the <em>clásico</em> on Sunday night, Real Madrid’s manager hardly moved, sitting in the shadow of the bench – but when the striker got the second to win it with time running out, that was different. Mourinho leapt into the light, throwing himself to the grass, the knees of a 63-year-old’s trousers muddy as a schoolboy’s, stuck his tongue out and pumped his fists.</p><p>He does so love it when a plan comes together. To the right of him, the bench was emptying, subs joining the players in sprinting towards the south-west corner. As they leapt about, dodging the bottles thrown towards them from the end, way, way up in the furthest corner and stuck inside a glass box like a bunch of David Blaines, the small group of Madrid fans who had come were going mad. In the main stand, a thousand phones were raised. And 600 kilometres west, back in Boadilla, Thibaut Courtois was watching his teammates from the sofa at home, presumably wrapped in a blanket and cradling a cup of Lemsip. On the morning of the biggest game there is, he awoke with flu, forced to miss out.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/oct/26/mourinhos-plan-comes-together-as-real-madrid-relaunch-with-clasico-statement">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/info/2022/nov/14/football-daily-email-sign-up"><strong>Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now!</strong></a></p><p>Considering they’d just gone nine games without a win, assorted Manchester United fans carping about the manner of their team’s Bigger Cup win over Roma on shouty radio phone-ins on Tuesday night struck Football Daily as the type who’d complain about a firefighter refusing to wipe their boots at the front door before rescuing them from a burning house. Yes, it’s true that United played appallingly in the first half and were lucky to be only 2-0 down. And yes, the penalty was somewhat fortuitous against a knack-ravaged Serie A side <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/oct/14/champions-league-mourinhos-real-madrid-stage-crazy-comeback-on-roma-return">who have form</a> in coughing up two-goal leads in the competition. However, when your once mighty side has spent the opening months of the season looking more like a broken washing machine full of spanners falling down an escalator than an elite football team, complaining about the artistic merit of a highly unlikely comeback win seems unnecessarily churlish, even if Matheus Cunha’s celebration of the winner was a little over the top.</p><p>Roma managed to capitulate to Manchester United while being 2-0 up. Even Man Utd haven’t managed to do that too many times but I wouldn’t describe their second half performance as ‘<a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/nov/03/manchester-united-roma-champions-league-match-report">a comeback for the ages</a>’. Their opponents just didn’t turn up” – Nigel Sanders.</p><p>These suggestions of paper and velcro shirts seem overly complicated. (<a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/nov/03/west-ham-scott-parker-football-daily-newsletter">yesterday’s Football Daily letters</a>). If teams would just commit to using body paint instead of clothing, the foul becomes impossible to commit unless a defender is possessed of both long fingernails and a cavalier disregard for the health of their opponent. Also, no more tedious yellow cards for removing the shirt after a goal. Win win” – Ben Mimmack.</p><p>Poor Nuno can take comfort that he’s in a long list of managers seen off by a poor result against West Brom since 2010, including Chris Hughton twice and five others. If you add Roberto di Matteo (he clung on for one more game) and spoiling Alex Ferguson’s leaving do with a 5-5 draw we were responsible for nine dismissals in seven years between 2010 and 2017. I think that’s pretty impressive. We’ve been quiet since then but perhaps we’re going for another run – championship managers beware” – Tom Levesley.</p><p><em><strong>This is an extract from our daily football email … Football Daily.       <title>Ousmane Dembélé quietly becomes the main man after long journey to the top</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/football/2025/dec/20/ousmane-dembele-quietly-becomes-the-main-man-after-long-journey-to-the-top</link>
      <description><p>The Frenchman, who has been named the best male footballer in the world by the Guardian, has benefitted from PSG’s focus on the team rather than individuals</p><p>What makes a good player great, and a great player the best? This question has been occupying me since 2014, when the Guardian first asked me to contribute to its <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/blog/ng-interactive/2014/oct/14/next-generation-2014-40-of-the-best-young-talents-in-world-football">inaugural Next Generation feature</a>. My job was to look for a France-based talent born in 1997 who could go on to have a stellar career.</p><p>After a great deal of research, I narrowed it down from my shortlist&nbsp;of five by asking questions&nbsp;not about the players’ football ability, but about other attributes: resilience, adaptability, decision-making, creativity, work ethic, response to feedback and willingness to learn.       <title>Aitana Bonmatí makes Guardian top 100 history with third title in a row</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/football/2025/dec/05/aitana-bonmati-guardian-top-100-history-third-straight-title</link>
      <description><p>The margin may have got smaller but the brilliant Spanish midfielder makes it a hat-trick of No 1 finishes</p><p>They say the best things come in threes, and Aitana Bonmatí has written herself into <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/ng-interactive/2025/dec/01/the-100-best-female-footballers-in-the-world-2025">the Guardian’s top 100</a> history as the first player to finish at the top of the tree for a third consecutive year.</p><p>Last year the majestic midfielder emulated her Barcelona and Spain teammate Alexia Putellas by <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/ng-interactive/2024/dec/03/the-100-best-female-footballers-in-the-world-2024">winning for a second year running</a>, but the 27-year-old has now gone one better, establishing herself once again at the top of the women’s game.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/2025/dec/05/aitana-bonmati-guardian-top-100-history-third-straight-title">Continue reading...</a></description>
